battle.title: Bucket Brigade
battle.description: Collisions everywhere: probing, chaining and load factor under pressure.

options: The same key is inserted twice and overwrites its value
The table runs out of memory
A key's hash code is a negative number
Two different keys map to the same bucket index
questions.answer: Two different keys map to the same bucket index
questions.explanation: Collisions are unavoidable when more keys exist than buckets. Overwriting a duplicate key is normal map behaviour, not a collision.

questions.text: What does this linear probing program print?
questions.explanation: All three keys hash to 0; each collision moves to the next free slot, so they fill indices 0, 1 and 2. Answering [5, -1, ...] imagines later keys overwriting each other.

questions.text: A table gets many insertions and deletions and may hold more keys than it has buckets. Which collision strategy fits?
options: Linear probing in a fixed-size array without resizing
Separate chaining: each bucket holds a list of entries
Overwrite the older entry whenever a collision occurs
Reject any new key that collides
questions.answer: Separate chaining: each bucket holds a list of entries
questions.explanation: Chaining stores any number of keys per bucket and deletes by removing a list node. A probing table cannot exceed its slot count and needs tombstones for deletes; overwriting or rejecting loses data.

questions.text: In plain linked-list chaining with n keys, what is the worst-case lookup time when every key hashes to the same bucket?
options: O(n), because one list holds all the keys
O(1), because hashing finds the bucket directly
O(log n), because the bucket is binary searched
O(m), where m is the number of buckets
questions.answer: O(n), because one list holds all the keys
questions.explanation: Hashing finds the bucket in O(1), but then the list is searched linearly through all n keys. A good hash function and resizing keep lists short on average.

questions.text: Keys are hashed with k % 4 into a chaining table. What does this program print for the bucket sizes?
questions.explanation: Remainders are 0,0,1,1,1,2 for 4,8,1,5,9,2, giving counts 2,3,1 and bucket 3 stays empty. Assuming an even spread would give [2, 2, 1, 1].

coding.title: Chaining Bucket Sizes
coding.description: Simulate a hash table with separate chaining and m buckets. The hash function is h(x) = ((x mod m) + m) mod m, so negative keys land in a valid bucket. Insert the keys in order; a key already present in its bucket is ignored. Print the number of keys stored in each bucket, from bucket 0 to bucket m-1.
coding.inputDescription: Line 1: m and n. Line 2: n integers (keys).
coding.outputDescription: m integers separated by spaces: the bucket sizes.
